A flowering of Black American writing, music, art, theatre and thought centred on Harlem in New York City in the 1920s and 1930s. At the time it was called the New Negro Movement, after The New Negro, an anthology edited by Alain Locke in 1925.

It grew out of the Great Migration, as hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners moved to northern cities. Harlem became the largest Black community in the country. Writers and artists there set out to show Black life in their own voices, with pride and without apology. Among them:

  • writers Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Claude McKay and Countee Cullen
  • thinkers such as W. E. B. Du Bois, whose magazine The Crisis published new writers
  • musicians of jazz and blues such as Duke Ellington and Bessie Smith, at clubs like the Cotton Club
  • painters such as Aaron Douglas

The Great Depression ended much of its funding, and the Harlem riot of 1935 marked a turn. But its pride and voice fed later Black writing and the civil rights movement.
